title: 5 Octopus Secrets So Weird It Feels Like an Alien
description: This week a rare Dumbo octopus was filmed near Palau, and scientists in Vienna just found a new clue to how octopuses got their brains. We count down five octopus secrets, from blue blood and a heart that stops when it swims to the strangest mother in the ocean.

scenes.say: This animal has three hearts, blue blood, and arms that think for themselves.

scenes.label: Three hearts
scenes.say: And it's not from another planet. It's living in oceans all over the world, right now.

scenes.label: Five secrets
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the plan. Five octopus secrets, counting down. Each one is weirder than the one before.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: And stay to the very end. Because the last one is about an octopus mom, and it's the strangest story in the whole ocean.

scenes.label: This week
scenes.say: But first, why are we talking about octopuses right now? Because this week, a camera caught something very rare.

scenes.label: Near Palau
scenes.say: Scientists from the Ocean Exploration Trust and NOAA were exploring a seamount near the Palau Marine Sanctuary, deep in the Pacific.

scenes.label: A Dumbo octopus
scenes.say: Their robot's lights hit something pale, with two little fins flapping like ears. A Dumbo octopus.

scenes.label: Hold that thought
scenes.say: Before the dive, they'd joked they might see two. They saw one, and the team was still thrilled. Hold on to that Dumbo. It comes back later.

scenes.label: Blue blood
scenes.say: Number five. Its blood is blue. Not a little bit blue. Actually blue.

scenes.label: Copper, not iron
scenes.say: Your blood uses iron to carry oxygen. That's what makes it red. Octopus blood uses copper instead, in a protein called hemocyanin.

scenes.label: Hemocyanin
scenes.say: And copper-based blood looks blue. So if an octopus gets a scratch, what leaks out isn't red at all.

scenes.label: A weak system
scenes.say: Here's the thing, though. Pushing that blue blood around takes serious work. So the octopus didn't settle for one pump.

scenes.label: Two for the gills
scenes.say: It grew three hearts. Two of them pump blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen.

scenes.label: One for the body
scenes.say: The third heart pushes that fresh blood out to the rest of the body. The organs, the muscles, everything.

scenes.label: Heart stops
scenes.say: But here's the twist. When an octopus swims, that third heart stops beating. It just stops.

scenes.label: Rather crawl
scenes.say: That's why swimming wears an octopus out so fast. And it's why most octopuses would rather crawl along the bottom.

scenes.label: One heart off
scenes.say: Think about that. Every time it swims away from danger, it's doing it with one heart switched off.

scenes.label: Thinking arms
scenes.say: Number four. Its arms have minds of their own. And I mean that almost literally.

scenes.label: 500 million neurons
scenes.say: An octopus has more than five hundred million neurons. That's in the same range as a dog.

scenes.label: Two thirds in arms
scenes.say: But a dog keeps most of its neurons in its head. The octopus doesn't. More than two thirds are in its arms and body.

scenes.label: Arm decides
scenes.say: So each arm can make quick decisions on its own. Grab it, or keep searching? The arm decides.

scenes.label: Harvard, 2020
scenes.say: And those suckers aren't just for holding on. In 2020, Harvard scientists found special sensors inside them.

scenes.label: Taste by touch
scenes.say: They called them chemotactile receptors. Basically, the octopus tastes things by touching them.

scenes.label: Tasting the dark
scenes.say: Imagine sticking your hand into a dark hole and tasting everything you touch. That's how an octopus hunts.

scenes.label: Arms keep going
scenes.say: The Harvard team says the arms can still reach for, identify, and grab things even when they're no longer attached to the body.

scenes.label: Chicago, 2026
scenes.say: And just this August, scientists at the University of Chicago found that octopus arm nerves are built in repeating segments.

scenes.label: Suckerotopy
scenes.say: Each sucker even gets its own little map in the nerve cord. The team gave it a funny name. Suckerotopy.

scenes.label: Vienna, this month
scenes.say: So where did this crazy brain come from? Here's what scientists in Vienna found this month.

scenes.label: Folded DNA
scenes.say: It's not only about the genes. It's how the DNA is folded. Hundreds of millions of years ago, the octopus genome got rearranged.

scenes.label: A plausible clue
scenes.say: That brought far-apart pieces together, and may have opened new ways to switch on brain genes. The researchers call it regulatory entanglement.

scenes.label: Colorblind?
scenes.say: Number three. It's a master of color, but it's probably colorblind. Wait, what?

scenes.label: Instant disguise
scenes.say: An octopus can change its color and pattern to match a rock, a reef, or a patch of sand. Almost instantly.

scenes.label: Chromatophores
scenes.say: It does it with tiny color sacs in its skin called chromatophores. When they expand, the color spreads out across the skin.

scenes.label: One photoreceptor
scenes.say: But here's the problem. Octopus eyes have only one type of light-sensing cell. That's why scientists call them colorblind.

scenes.label: Two ideas
scenes.say: So how does a colorblind animal match colors this well? Nobody knows for sure. But there are two wild ideas.

scenes.label: UC Santa Barbara
scenes.say: Idea one. In 2015, researchers at UC Santa Barbara tested skin from a California two-spot octopus.

scenes.label: Skin that sees
scenes.say: When they shined light on it, the color sacs opened up. The skin reacted to light without any eyes involved.

scenes.label: Opsins in skin
scenes.say: They found light-sensing genes active in the skin, the same kind of protein used in eyes. So the skin may sense light by itself.

scenes.label: Father and son
scenes.say: Idea two comes from a father and son. Alexander Stubbs at Berkeley, and Christopher Stubbs, an astrophysicist at Harvard.

scenes.label: Dumbbell pupils
scenes.say: Octopus pupils come in strange shapes, like dumbbells. They think those pupils turn color into blur, and the octopus can read the blur.

scenes.label: Still testing
scenes.say: Is that true? Researchers are still testing it. But either way, the result is the same. You'd walk right past one.

scenes.label: Deepest octopus
scenes.say: Number two. Remember our Dumbo octopus from this week? It belongs to a family that goes deeper than any other octopus.

scenes.label: 6,957 meters
scenes.say: In 2019, a camera in the Java Trench filmed a Dumbo octopus almost 7,000 meters down. That's about 4.3 miles.

scenes.label: World record
scenes.say: That's more than a mile deeper than any octopus anyone had seen before. It's now a Guinness World Record.

scenes.label: Crushing pressure
scenes.say: Down there, the pressure should crush cells. The expedition's chief scientist said they'd have to do something clever inside their cells.

scenes.label: How big?
scenes.say: But going deep isn't the only record. Okay, so how big can an octopus get? You're not going to like this.

scenes.label: Hokkaido, 2026
scenes.say: In April, a team led by Yasuhiro Iba at Hokkaido University published fossil octopus jaws in the journal Science.

scenes.label: Up to 19 meters
scenes.say: Based on those jaws, the ancient octopus may have been up to nineteen meters long. That's about sixty-two feet.

scenes.label: Cretaceous Kraken
scenes.say: It lived between a hundred and seventy-two million years ago, in the age of the dinosaurs. Scientists nicknamed it the Cretaceous Kraken.

scenes.label: Top predator
scenes.say: And the adult jaws showed heavy wear. Iba said it was an active, intelligent predator at the very top of the food web.

scenes.label: The mother
scenes.say: Number one. And I warned you, this is the strangest. It's about a mother.

scenes.label: Monterey Canyon
scenes.say: In 2007, researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute sent a submersible down Monterey Canyon in California.

scenes.label: 160 eggs
scenes.say: About 1,400 meters down, clinging to the rock, they found a deep-sea octopus guarding about 160 eggs.

scenes.label: 3 degrees C
scenes.say: The water there is around three degrees Celsius. Dark. Freezing. Nothing but her and her eggs.

scenes.label: Still there
scenes.say: So they kept coming back. Thirty-eight days later, she was still there. Then months. Then years.

scenes.label: She refused
scenes.say: They even offered her a crab with the sub's robot arm. She refused it. As far as they could tell, she never ate.

scenes.label: 53 months
scenes.say: She guarded those eggs for fifty-three months. That's about four and a half years. The longest brooding period known for any animal.

scenes.label: What else?
scenes.say: And get this. The researchers wrote that it only seems extraordinary because we mostly study shallow-water octopuses. So what else is down there?

scenes.label: Built in
scenes.say: And when the eggs finally hatched, she was gone. Here's the part that sounds impossible. That ending was built into her body.

scenes.label: Optic gland
scenes.say: Octopus moms stop eating once they lay eggs, and they fade away by the time the eggs hatch. Scientists traced it to the optic gland.

scenes.label: 1977 experiment
scenes.say: In 1977, a scientist removed that gland from octopus mothers. They left their eggs, started eating again, and lived for months longer.

scenes.label: Chicago, 2022
scenes.say: In 2022, a University of Chicago team found the gland changes how the mom's body uses cholesterol after she lays eggs.

scenes.label: A countdown
scenes.say: So it's a built-in countdown. She gives everything she has to her babies, and her body is wired to let go.

scenes.label: Alien? Almost
scenes.say: Three hearts. Blue blood. Arms that taste. A colorblind master of disguise. And a mom who waits four and a half years.

scenes.label: Which one?
scenes.say: So which one surprised you most? Tell me in the comments. And if octopuses could live longer, would they rule the ocean?

short.title: This Animal Has 3 Hearts. One Stops When It Swims
short.header: Why the octopus is basically an alien
short.description: Octopuses have three hearts, copper-based blue blood, and two thirds of their neurons in their arms. One deep-sea mom guarded her eggs for 53 months. Sources: Smithsonian, OIST, Harvard (Cell 2020), MBARI via National Geographic.

scenes.say: This animal has three hearts, and one of them stops when it swims.
Its blood is blue, because it uses copper, not iron, to carry oxygen. Two hearts pump that blood through the gills.
The third heart sends it to the body. But when the octopus swims, that third heart stops. So swimming wears it out fast.
And its brain? More than five hundred million neurons, like a dog. But two thirds of them are in its arms.
Its suckers can taste what they touch. Harvard scientists found the sensors in 2020.
One deep-sea mom guarded her eggs for fifty-three months without eating. So is it an alien? No. It's an octopus.
So next time you think aliens aren't real, and an animal swims past you, just remember.
